lines: Cross the line, and your ride is on its way to the backend.
The race gave the ride an id when it started. At the line it sends the facts: map, place, seconds, distance, output, and the speed of every second.
A class does the same when it ends, with the bike's own speed for the distance.
The backend records each ride once. Send it again, and you get the first answer back, even when two copies race each other in.
And it checks the ride could be ridden: over two thousand watts, over a hundred kilometres an hour, or a distance its speeds don't add up to, and it's refused.
The app sends facts only. XP, stars and unlocks are the backend's to work out.
What the tests prove: once per ride id, refused when it can't be true, and sent the moment a ride ends.
Telo Ride, from the Telo family, turns a smart bike at home into a game.
It pairs with the bike over Bluetooth, reads your power and sets resistance for every hill and interval.

lines.text: Two doors: Race, ride a map against your best-time ghost, bots or people; and Classes, ride along to a video, alone or with a group; fed by one progression of XP, rider levels, stars and map unlocks.
